blocks.text: A pilot flying from Lagos to Kano cannot say "turn a bit to the right". Aircraft, ships and surveyors all use one unambiguous system: a three-figure bearing measured from north. Once you can sketch a bearing, the rest is the trigonometry you already know.

blocks.markdown:
A **bearing** is an angle that fixes a direction. Three rules define it completely:

1. Measure from **north**.
2. Turn **clockwise**.
3. Write the answer with **three figures**, so 7° becomes 007° and 45° becomes 045°.

So a bearing is always a number from 000° to 360°.

blocks.title: Bearing of B from A
blocks.text: Stand at **A**, face **north**, then turn clockwise until you are facing **B**. The angle you have turned through is the bearing of B from A. The order of the letters tells you where to stand — "the bearing of B **from** A" means the north line is drawn at A.

blocks.caption: The eight compass directions as bearings — worth memorising

blocks.markdown:
### Back bearings

If the bearing of B from A is known, the **back bearing** (the bearing of A from B) points the opposite way, so the two differ by exactly 180°:

- If the bearing is **less than 180°**, **add** 180°.
- If the bearing is **180° or more**, **subtract** 180°.

So the back bearing of 070° is 070° + 180° = **250°**, and the back bearing of 210° is 210° − 180° = **030°**. Notice how the second answer still needs its leading zero.

blocks.title: North then east: distance and bearing
blocks.prompt: A surveyor walks 5 km due north from P to Q, then 12 km due east from Q to R. Find (a) the distance PR and (b) the bearing of R from P, to the nearest degree.

steps.text: Sketch it. The north leg and the east leg meet at Q at a right angle, so triangle PQR is right-angled at Q.
Use Pythagoras for the distance PR.
For the bearing, the angle at P is measured from the north line PQ, turning clockwise towards R. In the right-angled triangle the opposite side is QR = 12 and the adjacent side is PQ = 5.
Write it as a three-figure bearing.

blocks.answer: PR = 13 km and the bearing of R from P is about 067°

blocks.markdown:
### Resolving a journey into north and east parts

A journey of $d$ km on a bearing $\theta$ (where $\theta$ is less than 90°) splits into:

- distance **north** $= d\cos\theta$
- distance **east** $= d\sin\theta$

The cosine goes with the north part because the bearing angle is measured **from the north line**, so north is the adjacent side. For example, a ship sailing 20 km on a bearing of 060° travels $20\sin 60° \approx 17.32$ km east and $20\cos 60° = 10$ km north.

For bearings past 090° work with the acute angle to the nearer north–south line and decide the direction from your sketch. A journey of 15 km on a bearing of 120° makes an angle of $180° - 120° = 60°$ with the **south** line, so it goes $15\cos 60° = 7.5$ km south and $15\sin 60° \approx 12.99$ km east.

items: Draw a rough sketch — never attempt a bearing question without one.
Put a short north arrow at every point you are asked to measure a bearing from.
Mark the given bearings as clockwise angles from those north arrows.
Fill in the angles inside the triangle using alternate or co-interior angles between the parallel north lines.
Now choose your tool: Pythagoras and SOHCAHTOA if there is a right angle, otherwise the sine or cosine rule.
Convert the angle you find back into a three-figure bearing at the end.

blocks.title: Using angles between parallel north lines
blocks.prompt: B is 8 km from A on a bearing of 030°. C is 10 km from B on a bearing of 120°. Find the distance AC, correct to 1 decimal place.

steps.text: The bearing of A from B is the back bearing of 030°, which is 030° + 180° = 210°.
At B, the direction to A is 210° and the direction to C is 120°, both measured clockwise from the same north line, so the angle ABC is the difference.
The triangle is right-angled at B, so Pythagoras applies.

blocks.title: Three marks lost most often
blocks.text: Forgetting the leading zero (writing 45° instead of 045°), measuring the angle anticlockwise or from the east, and putting the north line at the wrong point. Reread the phrase "bearing of X from Y" and always draw the north arrow at **Y**.

blocks.title: The back bearing is not 360° minus the bearing
blocks.text: Subtracting from 360° reflects the direction in the north line, which is a different direction entirely. The back bearing differs by 180°, not by however much is left over from 360°. Check with an easy case: the back bearing of east (090°) must be west (270°), and 090° + 180° = 270° gives that, while 360° − 90° = 270° only agrees here by coincidence — try 070° and the two methods disagree.

points: A bearing is measured from north, clockwise, and written with three figures.
"Bearing of B from A" means the north line is drawn at A.
Back bearing: add 180° if the bearing is under 180°, otherwise subtract 180°.
A journey of $d$ on bearing $\theta$ (with $\theta < 90°$) gives $d\cos\theta$ north and $d\sin\theta$ east.
Sketch first, mark north arrows, then find the angles inside the triangle.
Use Pythagoras and SOHCAHTOA when there is a right angle, and the sine or cosine rule when there is not.
